title: Structured Interview Questions: How to Build a System That Actually Works
description: Build a structured interview from scratch: fixed question list, scoring rubric with anchors, calibrated interviewers, and a pre-written decision rule. Role-specific examples included.
metaDescription: How to build a structured interview from scratch: question types, scoring rubric, interviewer calibration, and the decision rule. Twice the predictive validity of unstructured.
keywords: structured interview questions, structured interview, structured interview process, structured interview rubric, structured vs unstructured interview
author: Harish Kumar
body:
A structured interview is one where every candidate gets the same questions, in the same order, scored against the same rubric, by interviewers trained to spot the same signals. It is the single most evidence-backed change a hiring team can make. Meta-analyses of decades of hiring research show structured interviews predict job performance roughly twice as well as unstructured ones, and they reduce hiring bias measurably.

This guide walks how to build a structured interview from scratch: the question types, the scoring rubric, and the operational details that make the difference between "we asked the same questions" and an actually structured process.

Why structured interviews work

Unstructured interviews fail in three predictable ways:

  • Interviewer A asks different questions than Interviewer B. Two candidates get two different interviews, and you cannot compare them.
  • The same answer scores differently depending on who liked the candidate. Halo effect: an interviewer who liked the candidate's opener rates every subsequent answer higher.
  • Pattern matching beats real evaluation. The interviewer subconsciously evaluates "is this person like other hires who worked out" rather than "does this person have the skills the role needs". That is where bias enters.

Structured interviews fix all three: same questions, same scoring scale, defined "great answer" anchors per question. Bias does not disappear, but the structure removes the easiest places for it to land.

The four building blocks

A structured interview has four parts. If any is missing, it is not structured, it is just consistent.

  1. A fixed question list. Every candidate gets the same questions in the same order.
  2. A scoring rubric. Each question has a 1 to 5 scale with pre-defined anchors for what each score means.
  3. Calibrated interviewers. Interviewers are trained on the rubric and reach roughly the same score when listening to the same answer.
  4. A decision rule. A pre-defined rule for how scores combine into a hire/no-hire decision (e.g., minimum 3.5 average across required dimensions, no score below 2 on critical dimensions).

Picking the question types

Three question types do the heavy lifting in structured interviews:

  • Behavioral. "Tell me about a time when..." Highest validity for predicting performance, because past behavior predicts future behavior.
  • Situational. "What would you do if..." Tests judgement on hypothetical scenarios. Useful for surfacing reasoning, lower validity than behavioral because candidates can rehearse answers.
  • Knowledge. "What is X?" or "How would you implement Y?" Tests skill directly. Critical for technical roles, optional for many others.

A good structured interview mixes 60 to 70% behavioral, 20% situational, and 10 to 20% knowledge. Adjust based on role: more knowledge for highly technical, more behavioral for management.

Writing the scoring rubric

The rubric is the hardest part to build and the most important. For each question, write the anchors before the interview happens.

Example: question is "Tell me about a time you had to influence a peer to do something they did not want to do."

  • Score 5 (exceptional): Specific recent situation. Names the peer's objection. Describes 2+ tactics they used to address it. Mentions a measurable outcome. Reflects on what they would do differently.
  • Score 4 (strong): Specific situation with clear tactics. Outcome is clear but may not be measurable. Some reflection.
  • Score 3 (acceptable): Generic situation, generic tactics. Outcome is fuzzy. Limited reflection.
  • Score 2 (below bar): Cannot recall a specific situation. Describes hypothetical instead. Or specific situation but no real tactics described.
  • Score 1 (unable to answer): Skips the question, refuses to answer, or gives an answer that suggests the situation never happened.

The anchors take 30 minutes per question to write the first time. The investment pays back across every interview round you run with that question.

Calibrating interviewers

Same question + same rubric does not equal same scoring. Two interviewers can hear the same answer and rate it 3 vs 5. Calibration is the fix.

The simplest calibration session: every interviewer reads three sample answer transcripts you have pre-scored (one weak, one mid, one strong). They score the transcripts independently. Then you compare and discuss disagreements. After 2 to 3 calibration sessions, interviewers usually agree within 1 point on the scale.

If you cannot afford full calibration, the cheapest version is the "two-interviewer" rule: every important question is heard by two interviewers, and you average their scores. This adds robustness without requiring formal calibration.

The decision rule

The last building block. Before the interview, write down what scores produce a hire.

A common decision rule for individual contributor roles:

  • Minimum 3.0 average across all rated dimensions.
  • No score below 2 on any "critical" dimension (e.g., communication, judgement).
  • At least one score of 4+ to demonstrate a real strength.

For senior roles, raise the floors:

  • Minimum 3.5 average.
  • No score below 3 on critical dimensions.
  • At least two scores of 4+.

The point is not the specific numbers. The point is that the rule exists before you hear the candidate, so you cannot adjust the criteria to fit the person.

What to keep, what to drop from unstructured interviews

Three things in unstructured interviews actually do help. Keep them.

  • The opening "tell me about yourself". Not for scoring. For settling the candidate's nerves so the scored questions start on better ground.
  • Candidate Q&A at the end. The questions they ask are themselves a signal: thoughtful candidates ask thoughtful questions. Just do not score it formally.
  • Off-topic small talk in the first 2 minutes. Same reason as the opener.

Drop:

  • "Walk me through your resume". You already read it. Use the time for scored questions.
  • Trivia questions and brain teasers. Almost no validity for predicting performance.
  • "Sell me this pen" style stress tests. Outdated and signals an aggressive interview culture that hurts your hiring brand.
  • Asking different candidates different questions. Same questions or you cannot compare.

Operational details that determine whether it actually works

Three details that separate "we have a structured interview" from "we have a structured interview that actually works":

  1. Same order of questions. Not just same questions. The order primes the candidate's mental state. Question 2 affects how they answer question 5.
  2. Interviewers score in real time. Not afterwards. Memory degrades fast and your overall impression bleeds into per-question scoring if you wait.
  3. Use a structured form for the notes. Free-form notes drift away from the rubric. A form with one field per question per dimension forces the interviewer back to the rubric. A simple interview evaluation form works.

The takeaway

A structured interview is the cheapest, highest-ROI change a hiring team can make. Four building blocks: fixed questions, scoring rubric with anchors, calibrated interviewers, and a pre-written decision rule. Start with one role, build the four pieces, run 5 interviews against it, and you will already see better signal than any unstructured process. Once it works, replicate to other roles.

Structured interview questions FAQ

What is a structured interview?
An interview where every candidate gets the same questions in the same order, scored against the same rubric, by interviewers trained on the same anchors. Decades of research show structured interviews roughly double the predictive validity of unstructured ones and reduce hiring bias.
How do you create a structured interview?
Four pieces: a fixed question list, a 1 to 5 scoring rubric with pre-defined anchors for each question, calibrated interviewers (who score the same sample answers similarly), and a pre-written decision rule for what scores produce a hire. Build the rubric anchors before the first interview, that is the hardest part.
How many questions should a structured interview have?
6 to 10 questions in a 45 to 60 minute interview. More than 10 and you run out of time per question. Fewer than 6 and you do not have enough data to score the candidate confidently. Pick the questions that map to the role's core requirements.
What types of questions go in a structured interview?
Behavioral (60 to 70%), situational (20%), knowledge (10 to 20%). Behavioral questions have the highest validity because past behavior predicts future behavior better than hypothetical answers. Adjust the mix based on role: more knowledge for technical, more behavioral for management.
How do you reduce hiring bias in structured interviews?
Three moves: define rubric anchors before the interview (not after, when bias creeps in), have at least two interviewers score important questions, and use a written decision rule for what scores produce a hire. None of this eliminates bias entirely, but it removes the easiest places for bias to influence the outcome.
Are structured interviews legal?
Yes, and they generally reduce legal risk compared to unstructured interviews. Structured interviews produce documented evidence of how candidates were evaluated, which helps defend against discrimination claims. Avoid questions about protected categories (age, religion, family status, etc.) in your structured set regardless of the structure.
